blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights this position paper from DeepMind, Google Brain, MIT, and the University of Edinburgh, which advocates for graph networks as a foundational building block for next-generation AI. The paper argues that human-like AI requires combinatorial generalization, which can be achieved through structured representations and relational inductive biases—constraints that guide learning algorithms toward better solutions by prioritizing relationships among entities. Modern deep learning's end-to-end approach, while successful, struggles with tasks like complex reasoning and transfer learning. The authors propose integrating structured approaches with deep learning to leverage both nature (end-to-end learning) and nurture (hand-engineered structure). The paper introduces the Graph Network (GN) framework, a unifying architecture for graph-based models that explicitly represents entities, relations, and global properties, enabling strong relational inductive biases and permutation invariance. The GN framework generalizes prior work like graph neural networks and message-passing neural networks, offering a flexible and powerful tool for modeling complex systems.
paper_title: Relational inductive biases, deep learning, and graph networks
paper_abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has undergone a renaissance recently, making major progress in key domains such as vision, language, control, and decision-making. This has been due, in part, to cheap data and cheap compute resources, which have fit the natural strengths of deep learning. However, many defining characteristics of human intelligence, which developed under much different pressures, remain out of reach for current approaches. In particular, generalizing beyond one’s experiences—a hallmark of human intelligence from infancy—remains a formidable challenge for modern AI. The following is part position paper, part review, and part unification. We argue that combinatorial generalization must be a top priority for AI to achieve human-like abilities, and that structured representations and computations are key to realizing this objective. Just as biology uses nature and nurture cooperatively, we reject the false choice between “hand-engineering” and “end-to-end” learning, and instead advocate for an approach which benefits from their complementary strengths. We explore how using relational inductive biases within deep learning architectures can facilitate learning about entities, relations, and rules for composing them. We present a new building block for the AI toolkit with a strong relational inductive bias—the graph network —which generalizes and extends various approaches for neural networks that operate on graphs, and provides a straightforward interface for manipulating structured knowledge and producing structured behaviors. We discuss how graph networks can support relational reasoning and combinatorial generalization, laying the foundation for more sophisticated, interpretable, and flexible patterns of reasoning. As a companion to this paper, we have also released an open-source software library for building graph networks, with demonstrations of how to use them in practice.
